Timely detection of memory attacks is critical, as delays can lead to further damage and compromised system integrity. Conventional solutions to address these threats, such as virtualization and sandboxing, incur significant performance costs and face challenges in detecting stealthy attack vectors. To address this, we propose a new approach, MDC, which leverages machine learning to enable near-instant detection of memory attacks at the hardware level. By identifying patterns in memory access patterns, MDC can pinpoint DOPs (Dynamic Memory Attacks) with high accuracy, even when the attack code is unknown. Our results show MDC's effectiveness in detecting a range of attacks, including ROP, RCE, and UBIK, achieving detection rates of up to 99% with minimal overhead, requiring only 0.5-1.5% of the memory access data. Our implementation of MDC on a Xeon server yields a maximum overhead of 5.7% and memory access of 1.07%. Furthermore, MDC's low memory requirements make it suitable for use in resource-constrained systems. By employing a novel machine learning-based approach, MDC enables the identification of memory attacks at the hardware level, eliminating the need for expensive virtualization solutions. In this research, we present a novel MT-DRL algorithm called Multi-Task Q-Learning (MTQL), which enables learning and knowledge transfer across different tasks. is characterized by an abrupt shift from a passive to an oscillating state
upon exposure to a sufficient stimulus. In this study, we introduce a novel
method for creating an excitable optical system within a silicon-based photonic
platform, consisting of a silicon nanowire incorporating a silicon-vacancy 
defect. By investigating the interaction between light and the excited state of 
the defect, we have found that the system exhibits properties typical of an
excitable optical system. Notably, we have observed a significant enhancement of
the defect's emission intensity in response to increased stimulus intensity,
followed by a return to baseline when the stimulus intensity falls below a 
critical threshold. Furthermore, we have successfully generated traveling waves 
across a silicon nanowire, and our findings are in line with the theoretical
predictions provided by the Hodgkin-Huxley model. These findings open up new 
possibilities for creating optical systems that can mimic biological processes,
and for developing innovative optical devices within silicon-based photonic 
platforms. The results presented here also pave the way for further research into
the potential applications of excitable optical systems in the fields of
optical communication, information processing, and optical metrology.
